questions.title: What makes a system distributed
questions.prompt: In your own words, what is a distributed system, and why is the lack of shared memory and a shared clock the thing that actually makes it hard to reason about, rather than just having more machines?
questions.modelAnswer: A distributed system is a collection of independent computers, each with its own memory, its own clock, and its own independent chance of failing, that coordinate with each other only over a network so that, to users and programs, they appear as one coherent system. The hard part isn't the number of machines -- it's that no node can directly observe another node's internal state, only infer it from messages that can be delayed, lost, duplicated, or reordered, and any node can fail without the others knowing immediately. That absence of shared state and a shared clock is exactly why problems like knowing 'what happened first' or 'is that other node actually dead' are genuinely hard, not incidental details.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as independent computers that only know about each other through messages over a network, with no shared memory and no shared clock. The reason that's hard, rather than just 'more computers,' is that every one of those assumptions I take for granted on a single machine -- that I can read a variable's current value, that events have an agreed order, that a crashed process is immediately visible as crashed -- stops being true the moment coordination happens over a network. A node going silent could mean it's slow, the message got dropped, or it's actually dead, and from the outside those look identical. Everything else in distributed systems, consensus, consistency models, failure detection, is really just different policies for coping with that one underlying fact.
commonMistakes: Thinking more machines automatically means more raw power without added complexity
Assuming network messages arrive quickly, in order, and exactly once
Confusing parallel computing on shared memory with a genuinely distributed system
Assuming failures are correlated or announced, rather than independent and often silent
keyPoints: Independent computers, each with their own memory and clock, coordinating only over a network
No shared memory and no shared clock between nodes
Failures happen independently and are not directly observable, only inferred from messages
The system still needs to appear as one coherent system to the people and programs using it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why the lack of shared memory/clock creates real difficulty

questions.title: What autograd actually tracks
questions.prompt: When you call loss.backward() in PyTorch, what is actually happening under the hood, and why does every parameter need requires_grad=True for this to work?
questions.modelAnswer: As tensors flow through operations, PyTorch builds a dynamic computational graph on the fly, but only for tensors that have requires_grad=True (or are derived from one) -- each such tensor gets a grad_fn recording how it was produced. Calling loss.backward() walks that graph backwards from the loss, applying the chain rule at each step to compute how much each parameter contributed to the loss, and populates the .grad attribute of every leaf tensor with requires_grad=True along the way. A tensor without requires_grad=True never gets a node in that graph in the first place, so there's nothing for backward() to compute a gradient for -- it simply isn't tracked.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as PyTorch quietly building a record of every operation as it happens, but only for tensors it's been told to care about via requires_grad=True. The moment I call loss.backward(), it walks that recorded graph in reverse, applying the chain rule at each step, and drops the result into .grad on every leaf parameter that was actually part of the graph. If I forget requires_grad=True on something, it's not that the gradient comes out wrong -- it's that no graph node was ever created for it, so there's nothing to differentiate. backward() itself doesn't update any weights either; it only fills in .grad, and a separate optimizer.step() call is what actually applies the update.
commonMistakes: Thinking loss.backward() updates the model's weights directly
Forgetting that .grad accumulates across calls, causing unexpectedly large gradients without zero_grad()
Assuming torch.no_grad() permanently disables tracking rather than just inside its block
Confusing leaf tensors, which actually receive .grad, with intermediate tensors in the graph
keyPoints: A dynamic computational graph is built as operations execute, only for tracked tensors
backward() walks that graph in reverse, applying the chain rule
Only leaf tensors with requires_grad=True end up with a populated .grad
optimizer.step() is a separate call that actually applies the update using .grad

questions.title: Why GPUs beat CPUs for matrix math
questions.prompt: A GPU has thousands of small, relatively slow cores while a CPU has a handful of large, fast ones. Why does that tradeoff favor the GPU specifically for neural network training, and where would it NOT help?
questions.modelAnswer: Operations like matrix multiplication and convolution are data-parallel: the exact same instruction (multiply, add) needs to run on huge numbers of independent data elements. A GPU organizes its cores into warps of 32 threads executing the same instruction in lockstep (SIMT), so sheer parallel core count applied to that kind of work dominates even though each individual GPU core runs at a lower clock speed than a CPU core. It does not help for inherently sequential logic, or for code with heavy per-thread branching, since threads within the same warp that take different branches force the warp to execute both paths serially (warp divergence), erasing the parallelism advantage.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as a tradeoff between a few fast, flexible workers and thousands of simple, synchronized ones. Matrix multiplication and convolution are exactly the kind of work where you want thousands of workers all doing the identical simple operation on different numbers at once, which is what a GPU's warps of 32 lockstep threads are built for -- even though each individual core is slower than a CPU core. Where that falls apart is branchy, sequential logic: if threads in the same warp need to go down different paths, the hardware can't actually run them in parallel anymore, it serializes both paths and masks off whichever threads don't apply, so you lose exactly the advantage you were hoping for.
commonMistakes: Thinking individual GPU cores run faster per-core than CPU cores
Forgetting that heavy branching inside a warp causes serialized execution (warp divergence), not free parallelism
Assuming any workload automatically speeds up just by running it on a GPU
Ignoring that warp divergence specifically erases the advantage for branch-heavy code
keyPoints: The advantage comes from parallel core count on data-parallel work, not clock speed
Warps of 32 threads execute in lockstep (SIMT)
Matrix multiplication and convolution are the canonical data-parallel operations that benefit most
Sequential or heavily branching logic doesn't benefit, and can suffer from warp divergence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the architectural tradeoff behind the GPU advantage
Correctly identifies workloads that don't benefit

questions.title: Global memory vs shared memory
questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between a GPU's global (HBM) memory and its on-chip shared memory, and why would a kernel author deliberately move data into shared memory instead of just reading from global memory every time?
questions.modelAnswer: Global memory (implemented as HBM) is large and visible to every thread in every block, but it's the slowest tier in the GPU's memory hierarchy. Shared memory is small, physically on-chip, and scoped to a single block -- each block gets its own separate copy, and any thread in that block can read or write it quickly. A kernel that reuses the same piece of data across many threads in a block benefits from loading it into shared memory once and letting every thread in the block read it from there, instead of every thread independently round-tripping to slow global memory for the same value -- which matters a lot for memory-bound kernels where those round-trips, not the actual arithmetic, dominate runtime.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as two very different tiers: global memory is the big pool everyone can see but it's genuinely slow to access repeatedly, while shared memory is a small, fast scratchpad that only exists per-block. The reason to bother copying data into shared memory first is reuse -- if ten threads in a block are all going to read the same value, fetching it from global memory ten separate times is wasteful; fetching it once into shared memory and letting all ten threads read it from there cuts that down to one round trip. I'd also flag that this only pays off when there's actually reuse -- if each thread only touches a given value once, moving it into shared memory first is pure overhead with no benefit.
commonMistakes: Treating shared memory as if it were just a faster version of global memory available to everyone
Thinking local (per-thread) memory is fast, when it's actually physically stored in the slow global-memory space
Forgetting __syncthreads() is needed to safely coordinate reads/writes to shared memory across a block
Assuming moving data to shared memory always helps, even when it's only read once per thread
keyPoints: Global memory is large, slow, and visible to every thread across every block
Shared memory is small, fast, on-chip, and scoped to one block with its own separate copy
The benefit comes from reusing a value across many threads in a block, not from just moving data
__syncthreads() is needed to coordinate access to shared memory correctly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes global memory from shared memory
Correctly explains the reuse rationale for shared memory

questions.title: Why interconnect speed matters for multi-GPU training
questions.prompt: After every backward pass in multi-GPU data-parallel training, gradients need to be synchronized across GPUs. Why does the speed of the connection between GPUs (NVLink vs PCIe vs Ethernet) matter so much for how fast training actually runs?
questions.modelAnswer: Gradient synchronization (an all-reduce) happens after every single training step, not occasionally, so its cost is paid every step regardless of how fast the GPUs themselves computed the forward and backward pass. If the time it takes to move that gradient traffic over the interconnect is significant relative to the compute time per step, communication becomes the bottleneck no matter how fast the GPUs are. NVLink offers far more bandwidth between GPUs than PCIe, which in turn is far faster than a typical Ethernet link for GPU-to-GPU traffic -- so the interconnect choice directly determines whether adding more GPUs actually scales training speed close to linearly, or whether the cluster spends an increasing share of every step just waiting on communication.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out that synchronizing gradients isn't an occasional housekeeping task -- it happens after every backward pass, every single step. So whatever that synchronization costs gets paid repeatedly, and if the interconnect is slow, that repeated cost can end up dominating the step time regardless of how fast the GPUs computed. NVLink gives GPUs within a node a much larger pipe to talk through than PCIe does, and PCIe is itself much faster than typical Ethernet for this kind of traffic -- so the practical effect is that the same cluster, same model, same code can scale almost linearly with more GPUs on a fast interconnect, or hit a wall well before that on a slow one.
commonMistakes: Assuming adding more GPUs always scales training speed close to linearly regardless of interconnect
Ignoring the communication step entirely when reasoning about training speed
Thinking GPU compute speed alone determines overall throughput
Confusing GPU-to-GPU bandwidth (NVLink) with GPU-to-CPU bandwidth (PCIe)
keyPoints: Gradient synchronization happens every training step, not occasionally
Communication time can dominate step time regardless of GPU speed
NVLink offers far more bandwidth than PCIe, which is far faster than typical Ethernet for this traffic
Scaling efficiency depends on the ratio of communication time to compute time per step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why synchronization happens every step
Explains the interconnect bandwidth's impact on scaling

questions.title: Why the same feature can give different values twice
questions.prompt: What is training/serving skew, and why is it often caused by something as simple as two different pieces of code computing 'the same' feature?
questions.modelAnswer: Training/serving skew is a mismatch between the feature values a model saw during training and the values it actually sees at serving time. A common cause is code duplication: training computes a feature with one piece of code (often a batch SQL query over historical data), while serving computes 'the same' feature with a separate, latency-sensitive implementation, and because the two were written independently and evolve independently, they can silently drift apart -- different null-handling, different windowing, different rounding -- without anyone intending it. The model's offline evaluation metrics can look perfectly fine, since they're measured against the training-side feature values, while real production performance degrades because serving is feeding the model something subtly different. A feature store helps by defining feature logic once and serving it consistently to both an offline store (for training) and an online store (for serving).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe skew as the model being trained on one version of a feature and served a quietly different version of 'the same' feature in production. The sneaky part is that it often isn't a big, obvious bug -- it's something like a batch SQL query and an online function both computing 'average rating over 7 days,' written at different times by different people, with a subtly different null-handling branch. Offline metrics don't catch this because they're measured against the training-side values, which look fine on their own; it only shows up once the model is actually serving live traffic and getting a slightly different input than it was trained on. The real fix isn't a one-off patch, it's not having two implementations of the same feature in the first place -- which is exactly what a feature store is for.
commonMistakes: Assuming skew only comes from stale data, not duplicated feature-computation code
Assuming good offline metrics guarantee good online production performance
Not realizing the durable fix is defining feature logic once, not just monitoring for drift after the fact
keyPoints: Training/serving skew is a mismatch between training-time and serving-time feature values
A common root cause is duplicated feature logic in two independently maintained code paths
The two implementations can silently drift apart over time
A feature store addresses this by defining feature logic once, shared by both stores

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct explanation of the code-duplication root cause

questions.title: Why GPUs behave differently during prefill and decode
questions.prompt: During LLM inference, why is the prefill phase typically compute-bound while the decode phase is typically memory-bound, and what do TTFT and TPOT each measure as a result?
questions.modelAnswer: Prefill processes the entire input prompt in one parallel forward pass, which keeps the GPU's matrix-multiplication units busy the whole time, making it compute-bound. Decode generates output one token at a time, and each decode step has to read the entire key/value cache accumulated so far to compute attention, so the GPU spends more of its time moving data than doing arithmetic, making decode memory-bound. Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially how long prefill (plus any queuing delay before it) takes before the very first output token appears; time per output token (TPOT) is the per-step latency during decode, once generation has already started.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split it into the two phases the way the course does: prefill is one big parallel pass over the whole prompt, so the GPU's math units stay genuinely busy -- that's compute-bound. Decode is one token at a time, and every single step has to read the whole KV cache built up so far, so the GPU ends up spending more time moving that cache around than actually computing -- that's memory-bound, even though the GPU still looks 'busy' the whole time. TTFT is the user-facing number for 'how long until I see anything at all,' which is really prefill time plus whatever queuing happened before it even started; TPOT is 'how long between each word after that,' which tracks decode's per-step cost.
commonMistakes: Thinking decode is compute-heavy because tokens keep accumulating
Treating TTFT and TPOT as if they measure the same thing
Forgetting that queuing delay, not just prefill itself, contributes to TTFT
Assuming more raw GPU compute automatically fixes a decode-speed problem
keyPoints: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and is compute-bound
Decode generates one token at a time and is memory-bound due to KV cache reads
TTFT measures time until the first output token, including any queuing before prefill
TPOT measures per-token latency once decode has started

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound

questions.title: Why BF16 usually skips GradScaler but FP16 doesn't
questions.prompt: Both float16 and bfloat16 use 16 bits, but training in float16 usually needs a GradScaler while bfloat16 usually doesn't. What's actually different between the two formats that explains this?
questions.modelAnswer: FP16 allocates more of its 16 bits to the mantissa and fewer to the exponent, which gives it a narrow dynamic range -- small gradient values during backpropagation can underflow all the way to exactly zero, silently killing learning for those parameters. GradScaler exists specifically to prevent this: it scales the loss up before backward() so small gradients stay representable, then unscales the gradients before the optimizer step. BF16 instead keeps the same 8-bit exponent range as FP32 (sacrificing mantissa precision, not range), so the same gradients that would underflow in FP16 generally stay representable in BF16, which is why BF16 training usually skips GradScaler entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point to where each format spends its 16 bits. FP16 gives more bits to the mantissa for precision but only a few to the exponent, so its range is narrow -- a small gradient can quietly round down to zero during backward, and nothing errors out, it just silently stops learning for that parameter. That's exactly the problem GradScaler fixes: scale the loss up before backward so those small values survive, then unscale before the optimizer actually applies the update. BF16 takes the opposite tradeoff -- it keeps FP32's full exponent range and gives up mantissa precision instead -- so the underflow problem FP16 has mostly doesn't apply, and the standard practice is to just skip GradScaler with BF16.
commonMistakes: Assuming FP16 and BF16 have the same dynamic range just because both use 16 bits
Thinking GradScaler fixes precision loss in general rather than specifically preventing gradient underflow
Assuming BF16 is strictly better in every way, ignoring that it has less mantissa precision
Treating 'skip GradScaler with BF16' as a hard rule rather than a general convention
keyPoints: FP16 has a narrow exponent range and more mantissa bits
BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range and gives up mantissa precision instead
GradScaler exists specifically to prevent gradient underflow in FP16
BF16 generally avoids needing GradScaler because underflow is far less likely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the exponent/mantissa tradeoff between FP16 and BF16

questions.title: Why idempotency matters when a request is retried
questions.prompt: If a client doesn't get a response to a request and retries it, why can a non-idempotent operation cause real damage, and what does making an operation idempotent actually require?
questions.modelAnswer: A dropped response looks identical to a dropped request from the client's point of view -- it can't tell whether the first attempt actually succeeded and only the response was lost, or whether nothing happened at all. Retrying a non-idempotent operation, like 'add $100 to this balance,' risks executing it a second time if the first attempt had actually succeeded, resulting in $200 added instead of $100. Making an operation idempotent typically means attaching a unique idempotency key to the request so the server can recognize and ignore an exact duplicate, or redesigning the operation itself so it converges to the same end state no matter how many times it runs, such as 'set balance to $500' instead of 'add $100.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The core problem is that silence is ambiguous -- if I send a request and get nothing back, I genuinely don't know whether it succeeded and the response got lost, or whether it never went through at all. For something like 'add $100,' retrying blindly in that situation risks double-applying it if the first attempt actually landed. The fix is either attaching a unique idempotency key so the server can say 'I've already seen this exact request, ignoring the duplicate,' or redesigning the operation itself to be naturally safe to repeat, like setting an absolute value instead of an incremental one. I'd also note this isn't just a payments thing -- any retry logic in a distributed system runs into the same ambiguity.
commonMistakes: Assuming retries are always safe regardless of the operation
Thinking the server can always detect duplicates automatically without any extra mechanism
Confusing idempotency with simply having retry logic at all
Assuming idempotency keys only matter for payment systems
keyPoints: Silence after a request is ambiguous: success, failure, and a lost response all look identical
Retrying a non-idempotent operation risks double-executing it
Idempotency keys let the server recognize and ignore duplicate requests
Some operations can be redesigned to be naturally idempotent

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the ambiguity problem behind retries
Correctly explains how idempotency is achieved

questions.title: Write the five-step training loop body
questions.prompt: Write the body of a single PyTorch training iteration for one batch (inputs, targets) given model, loss_fn, and optimizer already defined -- the five canonical steps every training loop repeats.
questions.modelAnswer: The five steps, in order, are: optimizer.zero_grad() to clear leftover gradients from the previous iteration, outputs = model(inputs) for the forward pass, loss = loss_fn(outputs, targets) to reduce the error to a single scalar, loss.backward() to populate .grad for every parameter via the chain rule, and optimizer.step() to actually apply the update using those gradients. zero_grad() has to happen before backward() populates new gradients, specifically because .grad accumulates across calls rather than resetting automatically -- skipping it means each iteration's gradients add on top of the last one's instead of replacing them.
questions.professionalAnswer: I write this the same way every time: optimizer.zero_grad(), then outputs = model(inputs), then loss = loss_fn(outputs, targets), then loss.backward(), then optimizer.step(). The one step people forget is zero_grad(), and the reason it matters is that .grad doesn't reset itself between iterations -- it just keeps adding on top of whatever was already there, so without clearing it first, the second iteration's gradients would be a sum of two steps' worth, not the standalone gradient for that batch.
questions.example:
for inputs, targets in train_loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    outputs = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_fn(outputs, targets)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
commonMistakes: Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad(), causing gradients to accumulate across iterations
Calling optimizer.step() before loss.backward(), so there's no gradient to apply yet
Forgetting the forward pass has to run fresh every iteration, not reuse a stale output
Placing the update step outside the batch loop instead of once per batch
keyPoints: Correct order: zero_grad, forward pass, compute loss, backward, step
zero_grad() prevents gradients from accumulating across iterations
backward() populates .grad via the chain rule
step() is the step that actually applies the parameter update

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct order of all five steps

questions.title: Size a kernel launch for an array
questions.prompt: You need to launch a CUDA kernel to process an array of 10,000 floats, with a block size of 256 threads. Write the launch configuration (grid size calculation and the <<<...>>> launch) that ensures every element gets a thread, and explain why you'd still need a bounds check inside the kernel.
questions.modelAnswer: gridSize should be the ceiling of n divided by blockSize: (n + blockSize - 1) / blockSize = (10000 + 255) / 256 = 40 blocks. That launches addOne<<<40, 256>>>(d_data, n), which provisions 40 * 256 = 10,240 threads for only 10,000 elements. A bounds check like if (i < n) is still required inside the kernel because the last block over-provisions 240 extra threads whose computed index exceeds n -- CUDA has no automatic bounds enforcement, so without the check those threads would write past the end of the allocated array, which is undefined behavior rather than a compile or runtime error.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd compute gridSize as (n + blockSize - 1) / blockSize, which for 10,000 elements and a block size of 256 comes out to 40 blocks, and launch addOne<<<40, 256>>>(d_data, n). That gives me 10,240 total threads for only 10,000 elements, so the last block has 240 threads whose index is out of range. I always keep the if (i < n) check inside the kernel because CUDA doesn't protect me from this automatically -- without it, those extra threads would just write past the end of the array, and that's undefined behavior, not something that throws a clean error I'd notice right away.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the ceiling-division formula and under-provisioning threads, silently dropping elements
Omitting the if (i < n) bounds check inside the kernel
Assuming CUDA automatically skips threads whose index is out of range
Off-by-one errors in the grid size calculation
keyPoints: Grid size uses the ceiling-division formula: (n + blockSize - 1) / blockSize
The launch syntax is kernel<<<gridSize, blockSize>>>(args)
A bounds check prevents the last block's extra threads from writing out of bounds
CUDA provides no automatic protection against out-of-bounds writes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why the bounds check is necessary

questions.title: Write a minimal Slurm submission script
questions.prompt: Write a minimal sbatch script that requests 2 nodes, 4 GPUs per node, and a 2-hour wall-clock limit, then uses srun to launch a torchrun command across the allocation.
questions.modelAnswer: The script sets #SBATCH --nodes=2, #SBATCH --gpus-per-node=4, and #SBATCH --time=02:00:00 to request the resources and time limit, then calls srun torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 --nnodes=2 train.py to actually launch the job. sbatch submits the whole script to Slurm's queue and returns immediately, running whenever Slurm schedules it; srun is what actually launches the parallel step -- one copy of the command per node -- once that allocation already exists, which is why the script calls srun torchrun rather than torchrun directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the #SBATCH header with --nodes=2, --gpus-per-node=4, and --time=02:00:00, then the actual launch line as srun torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 --nnodes=2 train.py. The distinction I always keep straight is that sbatch just files the job and hands back control immediately -- it doesn't run anything itself -- while srun is the thing that actually executes a command across the nodes Slurm already allocated. That's why I never call torchrun directly in an sbatch script; I call it through srun so it actually launches on every allocated node, not just the one running the script.
commonMistakes: Calling torchrun directly inside an sbatch script instead of through srun
Forgetting --nodes or --gpus-per-node, under-requesting the needed resources
Writing the --time value in the wrong format
Confusing sbatch (queues the job and returns) with srun (launches the parallel step)
keyPoints: #SBATCH directives request nodes, GPUs per node, and a time limit
srun is what actually launches the parallel step once the allocation exists
torchrun's --nproc_per_node and --nnodes must match the requested allocation
sbatch submits and returns immediately; srun runs inside the allocation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the sbatch vs srun distinction

questions.title: Request a GPU in a pod spec and check why it's pending
questions.prompt: Write the resources block that requests exactly 1 GPU for a pod, and the kubectl command you'd run to see why a pod requesting a GPU is stuck in Pending.
questions.modelAnswer: The resources block is resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1. To investigate a pod stuck Pending, kubectl describe pod <pod-name> shows the scheduling events (such as FailedScheduling, with a message like 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu') that explain why -- Kubernetes treats a GPU request as a hard requirement, so the pod stays Pending rather than running without a GPU or on a degraded resource.
questions.professionalAnswer: The resource request itself is just resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 under the container spec. When I see a pod stuck Pending, my first move is always kubectl describe pod <pod-name> and scrolling to the Events section at the bottom -- that's where Kubernetes actually tells you why it couldn't schedule, usually a FailedScheduling event naming insufficient nvidia.com/gpu. I'd also point out this isn't a bug: Kubernetes treats a GPU request as all-or-nothing, so the pod just waits until a GPU actually frees up rather than running in some degraded state.
questions.example:
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1

# then:
kubectl describe pod my-training-pod

Using kubectl get pod instead of describe and missing the Events section entirely
Assuming a Pending pod indicates a broader cluster-wide problem rather than this one pod's scheduling constraint
keyPoints: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 goes under resources.limits
kubectl describe pod reveals the scheduling events explaining a Pending state
A GPU request is a hard, non-overcommittable requirement
Pending isn't permanent -- it resolves once capacity frees up

questions.title: Log params, metrics, and the model to MLflow
questions.prompt: Write the MLflow tracking calls needed inside a training script to start a run, log a learning_rate parameter, log a final val_loss metric, and log the trained model itself.
questions.code:
import mlflow

# fill in the tracking calls
questions.modelAnswer: with mlflow.start_run(): scopes everything to one tracked run; inside it, mlflow.log_param('learning_rate', 0.001) records the hyperparameter, mlflow.log_metric('val_loss', val_loss) records the result, and mlflow.pytorch.log_model(model, 'model') saves the trained model itself. log_param and log_metric write queryable key/value data to MLflow's backend store (a metadata database), while log_model saves the model artifact to the separate artifact store, which is why MLflow keeps those two stores apart in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always wrap the whole thing in with mlflow.start_run(): so everything gets attached to one run instead of floating outside any run. Inside that block, mlflow.log_param('learning_rate', 0.001) for the hyperparameter, mlflow.log_metric('val_loss', val_loss) once I actually have the result, and mlflow.pytorch.log_model(model, 'model') to save the model itself. I keep in mind that params and metrics are small, queryable metadata going into one store, while the model artifact is a large file going into a completely separate artifact store -- that split is exactly why a metadata query never has to scan through gigabytes of model weights.
questions.example:
import mlflow
import mlflow.pytorch

with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("learning_rate", 0.001)
    # ... training loop ...
    mlflow.log_metric("val_loss", val_loss)
    mlflow.pytorch.log_model(model, "model")
commonMistakes: Calling log_param/log_metric outside the start_run() block, attaching them to the wrong run or none at all
Logging a hyperparameter with log_metric instead of log_param, or vice versa
Forgetting to call log_model entirely, losing the actual trained artifact
Hardcoding a value in the log call instead of the actual variable used in training
keyPoints: mlflow.start_run() as a context manager scopes a single tracked run
log_param records hyperparameters
log_metric records results like val_loss
log_model saves the model artifact, separate from the metadata backend store

questions.title: Launch a vLLM server with 4-bit quantization
questions.prompt: Write the shell command to launch vLLM's OpenAI-compatible server for a model called meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, using bitsandbytes 4-bit quantization, on port 8000.
questions.modelAnswer: vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --quantization bitsandbytes --port 8000 starts the server with the given model, quantization backend, and port. bitsandbytes is the right choice here because it quantizes weights on the fly at model-load time with no separate calibration dataset or pre-converted checkpoint required -- which matters whenever you need something working immediately rather than waiting on a calibration pass.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --quantization bitsandbytes --port 8000. I reach for bitsandbytes specifically when I need it working right now with no calibration dataset on hand -- it quantizes at load time, no separate conversion step, unlike GPTQ or AWQ, which both need a calibration pass over representative data before they're usable. If I had time and a calibration set ready, I might reach for one of those instead for better compression, but that's a different situation than 'ship it now.'
commonMistakes: Confusing bitsandbytes (zero-calibration, load-time) with GPTQ/AWQ (require a calibration pass)
Forgetting the --port flag and landing on the wrong default
Misspelling or mis-specifying the --quantization flag's value
Assuming all quantization approaches require an offline conversion step first
keyPoints: vllm serve <model> starts the OpenAI-compatible server
--quantization bitsandbytes needs no calibration dataset
--port sets the listening port
Correct flag names and values matter for the command to actually work

questions.title: Guard a payment handler with an idempotency key
questions.prompt: Write a small Python function process_payment(idempotency_key, amount, seen_keys, apply_payment) that only actually applies the payment once per unique idempotency_key, even if called multiple times with the same key.
questions.modelAnswer: The function checks whether idempotency_key is already in seen_keys; if so, it returns early without applying the payment again. Otherwise, it records the key and calls apply_payment(amount). seen_keys acts as a durable record of already-processed keys -- in a real system this would be backed by a database with a uniqueness constraint, checked and recorded as close to atomically as possible, so that a retry with the same key is detected and ignored instead of double-applying the payment.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd check seen_keys first: if the idempotency_key is already there, I return immediately without touching the payment logic at all. If it's new, I record it and then call apply_payment. In a real production system I wouldn't trust an in-memory set for this -- I'd want that check-and-record step backed by a database with a uniqueness constraint, done as atomically as the database allows, so two near-simultaneous retries can't both slip through before either one gets recorded.
commonMistakes: Checking and recording the key non-atomically, leaving a race window for near-simultaneous retries
Storing seen_keys only in memory, losing the record on a process restart
Keying on something the client doesn't send identically on every retry
Applying the payment before checking whether the key was already seen
keyPoints: A unique idempotency key identifies one logical operation
Check-then-record should ideally be atomic in a production system
Duplicate detection prevents double-execution on retry
Durability of the seen-keys record matters, not just in-memory tracking

questions.title: Fix a gradient accumulation loop missing the loss scale
questions.prompt: This gradient accumulation loop is missing one line that keeps its effective learning rate from scaling with accum_steps. Add the missing line and explain why it's needed.
questions.code:
accum_steps = 4
optimizer.zero_grad()

for i, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(train_loader):
    output = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_fn(output, targets)
    loss.backward()

    if (i + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
questions.modelAnswer: The missing line is loss = loss / accum_steps, inserted right after computing loss and before calling backward(). Because loss.backward() accumulates gradients across however many times it's called before the next zero_grad(), not dividing by accum_steps leaves the accumulated gradient accum_steps times larger than intended -- which silently acts exactly like multiplying the learning rate by accum_steps, with no error raised anywhere.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd add loss = loss / accum_steps right after loss = loss_fn(output, targets), before loss.backward(). The reason it matters is that backward() just keeps summing gradients into .grad across however many micro-batches run before the next zero_grad -- without dividing the loss down first, those four micro-batches' gradients add up to something four times too large, which has the same effect as quietly running with a four-times-larger learning rate. Nothing crashes or warns you about this, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.
questions.example:
accum_steps = 4
optimizer.zero_grad()

for i, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(train_loader):
    output = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_fn(output, targets) / accum_steps
    loss.backward()

    if (i + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
commonMistakes: Dividing the already-accumulated gradient after the fact instead of the loss before backward()
Dividing by the batch size instead of accum_steps
Assuming optimizer.step() automatically normalizes for the number of accumulated micro-batches
Not realizing this bug produces no error or warning at all
keyPoints: loss.backward() sums gradients across however many times it's called before zero_grad
Dividing the loss by accum_steps before backward keeps the effective gradient correct
Skipping the division silently inflates the effective learning rate
This is a silent bug that raises no error

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the correct missing line and its placement
Explains why the division is needed
Notes that no error is raised otherwise

questions.title: Configure a DataLoader for pinned, async transfers
questions.prompt: Write the DataLoader configuration and the .to(device, ...) call needed to overlap each batch's host-to-GPU transfer with ongoing GPU compute, assuming the DataLoader otherwise already works.
questions.modelAnswer: The DataLoader needs pin_memory=True (and ideally num_workers set to something greater than zero), and the transfer needs .to(device, non_blocking=True). pin_memory=True pre-allocates each batch in page-locked memory so the GPU's DMA engine can transfer it directly without a staging copy; non_blocking=True on that pinned source lets the transfer run asynchronously instead of blocking. Both pieces are required together -- on an ordinary, unpinned tensor, non_blocking=True silently behaves synchronously anyway, so pinning without the async flag, or the async flag without pinning, gives none of the actual overlap benefit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set pin_memory=True and num_workers=4 on the DataLoader, and change the transfer to inputs.to(device, non_blocking=True). The thing I always keep in mind is that these two changes only help together -- non_blocking=True on a regular, unpinned tensor quietly falls back to behaving synchronously, because the driver still has to stage it through pinned memory first regardless. So if I only add one of the two, I don't actually get the overlap between the next batch's transfer and the current batch's compute that I was going for.
commonMistakes: Setting non_blocking=True without pin_memory=True and expecting async behavior anyway
Pinning every tensor in a program regardless of the real cost
Forgetting num_workers so CPU-side batch preparation itself becomes the new bottleneck
Assuming .to(device, non_blocking=True) always returns immediately regardless of source memory type
keyPoints: pin_memory=True pre-allocates each batch in page-locked memory
non_blocking=True enables asynchronous transfer
Both settings must be combined for the actual overlap benefit
An unpinned source makes non_blocking=True effectively a no-op

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why both are required together

questions.title: A training job runs out of GPU memory partway through
questions.prompt: A training job that worked fine at batch size 16 now throws a CUDA out-of-memory error after you bumped the batch size to 64, with no other code changes. What's the most likely cause, and what are two straightforward ways to fix it without buying more GPU memory?
questions.modelAnswer: Activations dominate memory in most training jobs and scale roughly linearly with batch size, so quadrupling the batch size (16 to 64) quadruples the memory needed to hold activations for the backward pass. Two straightforward fixes without more GPU memory: reduce the batch size back down and use gradient accumulation to reach the same effective batch size over several smaller forward/backward passes before one optimizer step; or use gradient checkpointing, which recomputes activations during backward instead of storing all of them, trading extra compute time for lower memory use.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess is activations -- they scale with batch size, and going from 16 to 64 is a 4x jump, which is a very plausible way to blow past available memory with no other code change. Without more hardware, I'd reach for gradient accumulation first: run smaller micro-batches, accumulate gradients across a few of them, and only call optimizer.step() once I've simulated the larger effective batch size. If that's still not enough, gradient checkpointing is the other lever -- it recomputes activations during the backward pass instead of keeping them all in memory, which costs some extra compute time but can meaningfully cut memory use.
commonMistakes: Assuming OOM always means the only fix is buying a bigger GPU
Not realizing activations, not just model weights, scale with batch size
Confusing gradient accumulation (reduces per-step memory) with gradient checkpointing (recomputes instead of storing)
Forgetting optimizer state (e.g. Adam's) is also a separate, real memory cost
keyPoints: Activations usually dominate memory and scale with batch size
Gradient accumulation lowers per-step memory while preserving the effective batch size
Gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory by recomputing instead of storing activations
A lighter optimizer is a separate, additional memory lever

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives at least two valid concrete fixes

questions.title: Training loss shoots up to NaN a few hundred steps in
questions.prompt: A model's training loss decreases normally for the first few hundred steps, then suddenly spikes and becomes NaN, and stays NaN for the rest of the run. What's the most common cause, and what's the standard first thing to try?
questions.modelAnswer: This pattern is the classic signature of exploding gradients, often triggered by too high a learning rate or an unusually large or unlucky batch pushing weights into an unstable region. The standard first thing to try is gradient clipping with clip_grad_norm_, which rescales gradients proportionally so their combined norm never exceeds a fixed ceiling, applied between loss.backward() and optimizer.step(). If clipping alone doesn't resolve it, lowering the learning rate is the complementary next step.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd immediately suspect exploding gradients -- a sudden spike to inf or NaN that stays NaN afterward (since NaN propagates forward forever once it appears) is exactly that pattern, and too high a learning rate is the most common trigger. My first move is adding gradient clipping, calling clip_grad_norm_ right after backward() and before the optimizer step, which caps how large the combined gradient norm is allowed to get. If that doesn't fully fix it, I'd also try lowering the learning rate itself, since clipping treats the symptom while a lower learning rate addresses the instability more directly.
commonMistakes: Assuming NaN loss always means a data bug rather than an optimization instability
Not checking whether the learning rate is simply too high for this model/data combination
Applying gradient clipping after the optimizer step instead of between backward() and step()
Restarting training from scratch instead of adding clipping or lowering the learning rate first
keyPoints: A sudden spike to inf/NaN that persists is the classic exploding-gradient signature
Too-high learning rate is the most common trigger
clip_grad_norm_ is the standard first fix, applied between backward() and step()
Lowering the learning rate is the complementary second lever

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies exploding gradients/high learning rate as the likely cause

questions.title: A multi-GPU job hangs with no error for several minutes, then dies
questions.prompt: A 4-GPU DDP training job appears to just freeze -- no progress, no error -- for several minutes, and then the process finally dies with an NCCL timeout error. What does this actually tell you about what happened, and where would you look first?
questions.modelAnswer: An all-reduce (or any NCCL collective) is synchronous across every participating GPU -- all of them have to arrive at the same collective call before any can proceed. If one GPU is stuck, unusually slow, or has silently crashed, every other GPU simply waits at that point with no error of its own, since nothing looks wrong from their side yet. NCCL's watchdog timeout is what eventually converts that silent hang into an explicit error after a set duration. The first place to look is the straggler: check nvidia-smi and each node's driver Xid error log for a hardware fault, and check whether one rank's data loader or preprocessing is unusually slow, since that rank would be the one arriving late to the collective.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from the fact that collectives like all-reduce are synchronous -- every GPU has to show up before any of them can move on. So if one GPU is dead or just slow, nobody else gets an error, they just wait, and the timeout error I eventually see could technically come from any rank, not necessarily the actual faulty one. My first move is checking each node's nvidia-smi and driver logs for an Xid error, and looking at whether one particular rank is consistently the one running behind -- maybe its data loader is slower, maybe its GPU is degraded. I wouldn't just restart the job blindly; I'd want to know which rank was actually the straggler first.
commonMistakes: Assuming the error message points directly at the actual faulty GPU
Treating the hang as a bug in the training script rather than checking GPU/driver health first
Not knowing NCCL's watchdog timeout exists specifically to convert a silent hang into an explicit error
Restarting the job repeatedly without investigating which rank was the actual straggler
keyPoints: NCCL collectives are synchronous across all participating ranks
A slow or dead GPU stalls everyone else with no immediate error on their side
The watchdog timeout converts a silent hang into an explicit error after a delay
Investigate the straggler rank's hardware health and data pipeline first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a hang produces no immediate error
Gives a sensible first diagnostic step

questions.title: p99 latency is fine at low traffic but terrible under load
questions.prompt: An LLM serving endpoint has a great p99 time-to-first-token at low traffic, but under a traffic spike the p99 TTFT balloons to several seconds while per-token latency barely changes. What does this pattern point to, and what's the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: A TTFT tail that blows out while per-token latency (TPOT) stays steady points at queuing delay growing nonlinearly as the server approaches saturation, not a slowdown in the model itself -- requests are waiting for GPU admission or batch formation before model execution even starts. The fix is on the capacity side, not the model side: raise the number of replicas or the batch/concurrency ceiling so fewer requests queue, rather than trying to make the model itself faster through quantization or kernel tuning.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since TPOT barely moves while TTFT's tail blows out, that tells me the model itself is running fine once it actually starts on a request -- the problem is requests sitting in a queue waiting to be admitted before generation even begins. That's a capacity problem, not a model-speed problem, so I wouldn't reach for quantization or kernel optimization here; I'd look at adding more replicas or raising the concurrency ceiling so fewer requests pile up during a spike.
commonMistakes: Assuming a latency spike always means the model got slower, reaching for quantization first
Not distinguishing TTFT (includes queuing) from TPOT (decode-step latency) when diagnosing
Ignoring autoscaling lag as the real cause of the spike's timing
Assuming the fix must be code-level rather than capacity-level
keyPoints: TTFT includes queuing delay before model execution starts
TPOT reflects decode-step speed once generation has already started
A TTFT-only blowout under load points to queuing/admission, not model slowness
The fix is capacity (more replicas or a higher concurrency ceiling), not model optimization

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses queuing as the cause
Identifies the right category of fix

questions.title: A GPU training pod has been Pending for ten minutes
questions.prompt: A pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 has been stuck in Pending status for ten minutes. What's the most likely explanation, how would you confirm it, and is this something to escalate immediately or just wait out?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely explanation is that no node in the cluster currently has a free GPU -- Kubernetes treats a GPU resource request as a hard requirement, so rather than running the pod without a GPU or on a degraded resource, it leaves it Pending until capacity frees up. Confirm by running kubectl describe pod and checking for a FailedScheduling event mentioning insufficient nvidia.com/gpu, and checking GPU allocatable versus allocated counts across nodes. Whether to escalate or wait depends on whether other jobs are expected to free GPUs soon (fine to wait) or the cluster is genuinely undersized for current demand (worth escalating to whoever owns capacity), since nothing fixes itself just by waiting if there isn't enough capacity anywhere.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess is simply that there's no free GPU right now -- Kubernetes won't schedule a pod with a hard GPU request onto a node that can't satisfy it, so it just sits Pending. I'd confirm with kubectl describe pod and read the Events section for a FailedScheduling message naming insufficient nvidia.com/gpu, and check how many GPUs are allocated versus available across the nodes. Whether I escalate depends entirely on context -- if I know other jobs are about to finish and free up GPUs, I'd just wait; if the cluster is genuinely out of capacity for the foreseeable future, that's worth flagging to whoever owns cluster capacity rather than letting it sit silently.
commonMistakes: Assuming Pending always means something is broken rather than simply full capacity
Not checking the pod's Events section for the actual FailedScheduling reason
Assuming the pod will eventually run with degraded resources instead of waiting indefinitely
Escalating immediately without first confirming it's actually a capacity issue
keyPoints: A GPU request is a hard scheduling requirement with no fallback
kubectl describe pod's Events reveal FailedScheduling/insufficient-GPU
Check node-level GPU allocatable vs allocated to confirm
Escalation decision depends on whether capacity is expected to free up soon

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives the correct diagnostic command and what to look for

questions.title: GPU utilization is low even though the model trains correctly
questions.prompt: nvidia-smi shows the GPU sitting at only 30-40% utilization during training, bouncing up and down, even though the model is learning correctly and there's no error. What's the likely culprit, and what two settings would you check first?
questions.modelAnswer: GPU utilization that bounces between low and high, rather than staying consistently near 100%, is a classic sign the data pipeline (CPU-side loading and preprocessing) can't keep up, so the GPU sits idle waiting for the next batch between bursts of work. The two settings to check first are num_workers (too few workers means batches aren't prepared fast enough in parallel) and whether pin_memory=True plus non_blocking=True transfers are being used to overlap the host-to-GPU copy with compute instead of blocking on it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Bouncing utilization instead of a steady near-100% line almost always points me at the data pipeline before I even look at the model. The first thing I'd check is num_workers -- if it's too low, the CPU just can't prepare batches fast enough to keep the GPU fed. The second is whether pin_memory and non_blocking transfers are actually set up, since without them the GPU can end up waiting on the host-to-device copy instead of overlapping it with compute. I'd confirm with a quick batch-timing check or a profiler trace before changing anything, rather than guessing.
commonMistakes: Assuming low GPU utilization always means the model itself is too small or inefficient
Jumping straight to faster GPUs instead of checking the data pipeline first
Assuming more num_workers is always better, when too many can hurt due to CPU contention
Forgetting that CPU-bound preprocessing, not just worker count, can be the real bottleneck
keyPoints: Bouncing, sub-100% GPU utilization often points at a CPU-bound data pipeline, not the model
Check num_workers first
Check pin_memory and non_blocking for transfer overlap
Confirm with batch timing or a profiler rather than guessing

Names the correct settings to check

questions.title: One slow dependency is taking down an unrelated service
questions.prompt: Your inference gateway calls both a fast feature-lookup service and a slow, occasionally-overloaded logging service. Lately, when the logging service gets slow, the entire gateway -- including requests that don't even need logging -- starts timing out. What's going wrong, and what pattern would you reach for to fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a cascading failure caused by a shared, exhaustible resource -- calls to the slow logging service are tying up resources, like a shared thread pool or connection pool, that unrelated requests also depend on, so one dependency's slowness spreads to parts of the system that never even touch it. The fix is the bulkhead pattern: give the logging-service calls their own isolated, limited resource pool so that pool filling up only blocks requests that actually need logging, while feature-lookup and everything else keeps flowing normally through its own separate pool.
questions.professionalAnswer: This looks like a cascading failure through a shared resource -- probably a thread pool or connection pool that both the logging calls and everything else are drawing from. When logging gets slow, those calls hold onto that shared pool longer, and eventually there's nothing left for requests that don't even touch logging. The pattern I'd reach for is the bulkhead -- give logging its own dedicated, bounded pool, separate from everything else, so a slow logging service can only ever exhaust its own pool, not the one feature-lookup and other requests depend on.
commonMistakes: Assuming the fix is simply making the logging service faster rather than isolating its blast radius
Not recognizing a shared thread/connection pool as the actual mechanism of the cascade
Confusing the bulkhead pattern with a circuit breaker, which stops calling a failing dependency entirely rather than isolating its resource usage
Applying a global timeout increase, which masks the symptom without fixing the shared-resource coupling
keyPoints: A shared resource pool lets one slow dependency starve unrelated requests
This is a cascading failure, not an isolated outage
The bulkhead pattern isolates each dependency's resource usage into its own pool
A circuit breaker is a related but distinct, complementary pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names and explains the bulkhead fix

questions.title: Offline metrics look great, production performance doesn't
questions.prompt: A model's offline evaluation AUC looks excellent, but once deployed, its real-world performance is noticeably worse. Investigation shows the training pipeline computes a feature with one SQL query and the serving path computes 'the same' feature with a different function entirely. What's this called, and what's the actual long-term fix, not just a patch for this one feature?
questions.modelAnswer: This is training/serving skew caused by code duplication -- two independently maintained implementations of what's supposed to be the same feature, drifting apart over time through things like different null-handling, windowing, or rounding. Patching this one feature's mismatch fixes the symptom but not the underlying problem; the real long-term fix is adopting a feature store (or an equivalent shared feature-definition layer) so a feature's logic is defined exactly once and served consistently to both the offline store used for training and the online store used at serving time, eliminating the possibility of two divergent implementations entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd call this training/serving skew, and the root cause here is specifically code duplication -- two separate implementations of what's meant to be the same feature, written at different times, drifting apart. I could patch this one feature to make the two match today, but that doesn't stop the next feature from having the exact same problem a few months from now. The real fix is architectural: a feature store that defines each feature's logic exactly once and serves it consistently to both training and serving, so there's structurally no way for two divergent implementations to exist in the first place.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a one-off bug to patch in isolation rather than a structural problem that will recur
Assuming good offline metrics are sufficient proof a model is production-ready
Not recognizing that a feature store's core value is exactly this single-source-of-truth guarantee
Monitoring for skew after the fact instead of architecturally preventing it
keyPoints: Training/serving skew caused by duplicated feature logic
Offline metrics can look fine while production performance degrades
A feature store defines feature logic once, shared by both training and serving
The long-term fix is architectural, not a one-off patch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names and explains training/serving skew
Correctly identifies the structural (feature store) fix

questions.title: nvidia-smi shows 95% GPU utilization, but the job is still slow
questions.prompt: nvidia-smi dmon shows sustained GPU (sm) utilization near 95% for an entire training run, yet the job is still much slower than expected. Why doesn't a high utilization number alone prove the GPU is being used efficiently, and what would you check next?
questions.modelAnswer: nvidia-smi's utilization metric only reports whether some kernel was running on the GPU at all during each sampled interval -- it says nothing about whether that kernel was doing useful, compute-heavy work (like dense matrix multiplication) or spending most of its time waiting on memory traffic, which can also show up as 'busy.' A GPU can sit at 95% utilization while running a badly memory-bound or otherwise inefficient kernel the entire time. The next step is a deeper profiler: Nsight Systems for the overall timeline to spot idle gaps or poor overlap, and Nsight Compute on the specific hot kernel to see its actual compute-versus-memory throughput breakdown and whether it's hitting a low fraction of peak FLOPs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't treat that 95% number as proof of anything other than 'something was running on the GPU most of the time.' It doesn't tell me whether that something was doing real compute work or just shuffling data around in a memory-bound kernel the whole time, and both can look like high utilization. My next step would be Nsight Systems first, to get the broad timeline and check for idle gaps or poor overlap between operations, and then Nsight Compute on whichever kernel is actually eating the most time, to see the real compute-vs-memory breakdown rather than guessing from a single device-wide number.

Not knowing device-wide, time-sampled utilization hides per-kernel inefficiency entirely
Jumping straight to buying more or faster GPUs instead of profiling first
Confusing GPU utilization with tensor-core/compute-throughput utilization, which are different metrics
keyPoints: nvidia-smi utilization only means something was running, not that it was running efficiently
It can't distinguish compute-bound from memory-bound kernels
Nsight Systems gives the broad timeline, Nsight Compute gives per-kernel detail
Profiling, not guessing, is the correct next step

Names the correct next diagnostic tools

questions.title: Picking the right feature freshness tier
questions.prompt: You're designing feature serving for a fraud-detection model that needs a feature updated within the last minute (transaction velocity), alongside features that only need to refresh daily (account age) and one feature that can only be computed using data present in the actual incoming request (device fingerprint of this request). How would you structure feature computation for these three cases, and why not use one approach for all three?
questions.modelAnswer: Use batch materialization for the daily account-age feature, since its freshness needs are measured in hours and a scheduled job copying values from the offline store into the online store is the simplest, cheapest option. Use streaming ingestion for transaction velocity, since sub-minute freshness requires a stream processor writing directly into the online store rather than waiting for the next batch window. Use an on-demand feature view for the device fingerprint, since it depends on data only available at request time and can't be precomputed into either store at all. Using one approach for all three would either be wasteful -- streaming infrastructure for something that only changes daily -- or simply wrong, since no amount of batch or streaming materialization can produce a value that only exists once the request itself arrives.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd map each feature to its own pattern rather than forcing one approach everywhere. Account age only needs batch materialization -- a scheduled job copying from the offline store into the online store on something like a daily cadence is plenty. Transaction velocity needs streaming ingestion, since sub-minute freshness means a stream processor has to write directly into the online store as events happen, not wait for the next batch run. And the device fingerprint can't be materialized ahead of time at all -- it only exists once the request itself arrives, so it has to be an on-demand feature view computed at request time. Forcing one pattern onto all three would either be overkill for account age or flatly impossible for the device fingerprint.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to streaming for everything 'to be safe,' adding unnecessary infrastructure cost and complexity
Trying to precompute the request-dependent feature ahead of time, which is architecturally impossible
Not recognizing that freshness requirements, not team preference, should drive the materialization pattern choice
Treating the online/offline split as a database choice rather than a freshness/latency-pattern choice
keyPoints: Batch materialization fits hours-to-days freshness needs
Streaming ingestion fits sub-minute freshness, writing directly to the online store
On-demand feature views handle request-time-only inputs that can never be precomputed
The right choice is driven by each feature's actual requirement, not one default pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches each feature to the right pattern
Correctly explains why one pattern doesn't fit all three

questions.title: Choosing data parallelism over model parallelism for a model that fits on one GPU
questions.prompt: Your team has 8 GPUs available and a model that comfortably fits in a single GPU's memory with room to spare. Why would you choose DistributedDataParallel over a model-parallel (sharding the model itself across GPUs) approach here, and when would that choice flip?
questions.modelAnswer: When the model already fits on one GPU, DDP is the simpler and typically faster choice -- each GPU holds a full copy of the model, processes its own shard of the data independently, and only synchronizes gradients via all-reduce at the end of each backward pass, with no need to split the model's layers across devices or introduce the extra cross-GPU communication model parallelism requires between layers on different devices. The choice flips once the model itself no longer fits in a single GPU's memory (or a single very large batch's activations don't fit), at which point some form of model, tensor, or pipeline parallelism -- or a combined approach like FSDP that shards both data and model state -- becomes necessary regardless of how fast DDP would otherwise be.
questions.professionalAnswer: With a model that fits comfortably on one GPU, I'd default to DDP every time -- every GPU just runs the whole model on its own slice of data and the only coordination needed is one all-reduce on the gradients at the end of each step. Model parallelism would add real complexity and extra cross-GPU communication between layers for zero benefit here, since there's no memory problem to solve. The thing that would actually flip my decision is memory, not GPU count -- the moment the model (or its activations at the batch size I need) stop fitting on a single device, DDP alone can't help anymore and I'd need to look at sharding the model itself, possibly with something like FSDP that blends data and model sharding together.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to model parallelism because it sounds more sophisticated, adding complexity with no benefit
Not recognizing that the deciding factor is memory, not GPU count or a desire for more distribution
Assuming DDP and model parallelism are mutually exclusive rather than combinable approaches
Forgetting DDP still has a real communication cost from gradient synchronization every step
keyPoints: DDP is the right default when the model fits on one GPU
DDP requires only gradient all-reduce, not per-layer cross-GPU communication
The deciding factor to switch to model/tensor parallelism is memory, not raw GPU count
FSDP-style sharding is a middle ground combining ideas from both approaches

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly justifies the DDP choice for this scenario
Correctly identifies when the choice would flip

questions.title: Choosing a quantization method under a calibration-data constraint
questions.prompt: You need to ship a 4-bit quantized version of a model into production this week, and you don't have a calibration dataset ready. A teammate suggests GPTQ because it tends to preserve more accuracy. What would you actually recommend, and what's the tradeoff you're accepting?

The tradeoff being accepted is that bitsandbytes generally isn't as compression-efficient or as fast at inference as a properly calibrated GPTQ or AWQ model would be; the plan should be to ship with bitsandbytes now and revisit GPTQ or AWQ once a calibration set exists and there's time to validate it properly, rather than delaying the deadline to build calibration data from scratch.
