questions.title: Choosing storage for a large, shared training dataset
questions.prompt: You're setting up storage for a dataset that needs to be read concurrently by dozens of training workers across multiple nodes, at high throughput, but doesn't need to be edited in place. Would you reach for block storage (like an EBS volume), object storage (like S3), or a parallel filesystem, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Block storage is out immediately, since it attaches to a single instance and can't serve as shared storage across many nodes at once. Between object storage and a parallel filesystem, object storage (S3) is the natural home for the dataset itself -- cheap, durable, and its aggregate throughput scales horizontally across many prefixes -- but each individual request carries real latency, commonly tens of milliseconds, which can become a bottleneck for many small, concurrent reads during training. A parallel filesystem (such as FSx for Lustre) layered on top, lazily loading objects from S3 on first read and then serving subsequent reads from its own low-latency storage, gives the best of both: S3's durability and cost as the source of truth, with the parallel filesystem's low per-request latency for the actual training workload.
questions.professionalAnswer: Block storage is off the table right away -- it's tied to one instance, and this needs to be read by dozens of workers across multiple nodes at once. Between object storage and a parallel filesystem, I'd put the dataset in S3 as the durable, cost-efficient source of truth, since its aggregate throughput scales well with more prefixes. But I wouldn't stop there if the training throughput demands it, because each individual S3 request still carries real latency, often tens of milliseconds, which adds up across many small concurrent reads. Layering something like FSx for Lustre on top, which lazily pulls from S3 on first read and serves from its own fast storage after that, gives me S3's durability with much lower per-request latency for the actual training loop.
commonMistakes: Picking block storage because it feels simpler, without considering the multi-node sharing requirement
Treating object storage alone as sufficient without accounting for its per-request latency under many small concurrent reads
Not knowing a parallel filesystem can be layered on top of object storage rather than duplicating the data separately
Assuming local NVMe on each node could substitute for shared storage across nodes
keyPoints: Block storage can't serve multiple nodes at once
Object storage scales aggregate throughput but has real per-request latency
A parallel filesystem layered on object storage combines durability/cost with low-latency concurrent access
Local NVMe is for node-local scratch, not the shared dataset

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about the object storage vs parallel filesystem tradeoff

questions.title: Structuring a retraining pipeline's stages
questions.prompt: You're designing an automated pipeline that should retrain a model weekly on fresh data and also redeploy whenever the serving code changes. Sketch the stages this pipeline needs, and explain why a code deploy and a model deploy should usually be kept as separate, distinguishable events rather than one combined deploy step.
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline needs roughly: a data-pull stage triggered on a schedule, a retrain stage producing a reproducible candidate model with pinned dependencies and a tracked run, an evaluation stage comparing the candidate against the current production model on a fixed holdout set, and a promotion stage that only proceeds if the candidate passes the quality gate, alerting a human otherwise -- this is the continuous training (CT) piece, distinct from the continuous integration/delivery (CI/CD) piece handling serving-code changes triggered by a commit. Keeping code deploys and model deploys as separate, distinguishable events matters because if something breaks in production, you need to be able to tell which of the two actually changed -- a code deploy that coincided with a model promotion makes root-causing an incident much harder than if only one of the two happened at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd sketch two parallel tracks rather than one combined pipeline: a scheduled CT track that pulls fresh data, retrains a reproducible candidate, evaluates it against the current production model on a fixed holdout set, and only promotes if it actually passes that gate, alerting a human if it doesn't; and a code-triggered CI/CD track that handles serving-code changes on commit. I'd deliberately keep those as separate, distinguishable events rather than bundling them into one deploy, because the moment something breaks in production, I want to be able to say 'was this the new model or the new code,' and that's only possible if they didn't change at exactly the same time.
commonMistakes: Collapsing CT and CI/CD into a single trigger/deploy event, losing the ability to isolate which change caused a problem
Forgetting the pipeline needs to support both a schedule trigger and a code-change trigger
Treating a passed evaluation as automatically meaning immediate deploy, with no human alerting path on failure
Not including a fixed, unchanging holdout set for fair comparison across retraining runs
keyPoints: CT (scheduled retraining, evaluation, gated promotion) is distinct from CI/CD (code-triggered deploys)
A validation gate should stop the pipeline and alert a human on failure, not deploy anyway
Code deploys and model deploys should be separable events for incident diagnosis
The pipeline must support both a schedule trigger and a code-change trigger

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sketches the needed pipeline stages
Correctly explains why code/model deploys should stay separable

questions.title: Choosing a load-balancing strategy for LLM inference replicas
questions.prompt: You're load-balancing requests across several GPU replicas serving the same LLM, where requests vary widely in prompt length and expected output length. Why would plain round-robin routing be a poor fit here, and what would you use instead?
questions.modelAnswer: Round robin assumes every request costs roughly the same amount of work, which is a poor fit for LLM inference since prompt and output lengths vary widely -- a replica that happens to receive several long requests in a row ends up doing far more work than one that received short requests, even though round robin sent them equal numbers of requests. A better fit is least-outstanding-requests routing, which sends each new request to whichever replica currently has the fewest in-flight requests, naturally balancing actual load rather than request count; for multi-turn conversations, pairing this with session or prefix affinity, routing the same conversation back to the same replica, also lets that replica reuse cached context instead of recomputing it from scratch on a different replica each turn.
questions.professionalAnswer: Round robin's problem here is that it treats every request as equal cost, and with LLM inference that's just not true -- a long prompt or a long generation costs a lot more than a short one, so a replica can end up overloaded purely by bad luck in which requests it happened to get, even with a perfectly even request count. I'd use least-outstanding-requests routing instead, which actually tracks how much work each replica currently has in flight rather than just counting requests. And if this is a multi-turn chat workload, I'd also add session or prefix affinity on top, so a given conversation keeps landing on the same replica and can reuse its cached context instead of starting cold somewhere else every turn.
commonMistakes: Assuming round robin is fair because it distributes requests equally, without accounting for unequal per-request cost
Not considering that routing should account for in-flight load, not just a static rule
Forgetting that session/prefix affinity has a real benefit (cached-context reuse) that pure least-outstanding-requests alone would give up
Assuming any routing strategy works equally well regardless of workload cost variance
keyPoints: Round robin's equal-cost assumption breaks down with variable-length LLM requests
Least-outstanding-requests routing tracks actual in-flight load
Session/prefix affinity preserves cached-context reuse for multi-turn conversations
The right strategy depends on the actual cost-variance of the workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains round robin's flaw for this workload

questions.title: Why a cluster needs leader election rather than a fixed leader
questions.prompt: A team is designing a small coordination service and considers just hardcoding one node as 'the leader' permanently instead of implementing leader election. What would go wrong with that approach, and what would you recommend instead at a basic level?
questions.modelAnswer: Hardcoding a single node as the permanent leader creates an unmitigated single point of failure -- if that node fails or becomes unreachable, there's no mechanism for any other node to take over, and the whole system loses its coordination point until someone manually intervenes. At a basic level, the recommendation is a Raft-style leader election: followers expect regular heartbeats from the current leader, and if a follower's election timer expires with no heartbeat, it becomes a candidate, requests votes under a new term, and a candidate that wins a majority becomes the new leader -- all automatic, with each node voting for at most one candidate per term so at most one leader is elected for a given term.
questions.professionalAnswer: Hardcoding one node as the permanent leader basically bakes in a single point of failure with no recovery path -- if that one node goes down, nothing in the design lets another node pick up the role, so the system just stops coordinating until a human steps in. I'd recommend a basic Raft-style election instead: followers watch for regular heartbeats from the leader, and if one of them doesn't hear a heartbeat before its own election timer runs out, it becomes a candidate and asks for votes under a new term. Each node only votes for one candidate per term, so whichever candidate gets a majority becomes the new leader automatically, with no manual intervention needed.
commonMistakes: Assuming a hardcoded leader is simpler and therefore safer, without weighing the single-point-of-failure risk
Not recognizing that leader election specifically needs a majority-vote rule to guarantee at most one leader per term
Thinking leader election happens continuously rather than only in response to a missed heartbeat
Assuming any node can just declare itself leader without the voting/majority mechanism
keyPoints: A hardcoded leader is an unmitigated single point of failure
Leader election relies on heartbeats and an election timeout to detect leader failure
A candidate must win a majority vote to become the new leader
The majority rule guarantees at most one leader per term

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the risk of a hardcoded leader
Correctly describes the basics of heartbeat/timeout/election

questions.title: Designing a checkpointing approach for a large sharded model
questions.prompt: You're training a large model sharded across many GPUs using FSDP, and need a checkpointing strategy. Why wouldn't you gather the full model onto one GPU and save it with a plain torch.save, and what would you use instead?
questions.modelAnswer: Gathering the entire sharded model onto a single GPU before saving would require that one GPU's memory to momentarily hold the full model, and possibly optimizer state, while every other GPU sits idle waiting for the save to finish -- a serialization bottleneck and a real memory risk for any sufficiently large model. Instead, use a sharded checkpointing API like torch.distributed.checkpoint (DCP), where each rank saves only the shard of state it already holds, in parallel, along with metadata describing how the shards reassemble -- which also has the added benefit of letting a later load reshard onto a different number of ranks than the run that originally saved it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Gathering everything onto one GPU first means that single GPU has to momentarily hold the whole model, maybe the optimizer state too, which is exactly the kind of memory pressure FSDP was sharding to avoid in the first place -- and every other GPU just sits idle while that one does all the saving work. I'd use torch.distributed.checkpoint instead, where every rank saves only the shard it already has, in parallel, along with metadata describing how the pieces fit back together. That also means I'm not locked into reloading onto the exact same number of ranks I saved with, which matters if cluster size ever changes between runs.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a familiar plain torch.save without considering it requires gathering the full state onto one process first
Not recognizing the gather step itself as both a memory risk and a serialization bottleneck
Assuming a sharded checkpoint can only ever be reloaded onto the exact same number of ranks that saved it
Forgetting checkpointing needs to cover optimizer state as well as model weights
keyPoints: Gathering a sharded model onto one GPU before saving risks memory limits and serializes the save
Sharded checkpointing (e.g. DCP) lets each rank save its own shard in parallel
Sharded checkpoint metadata allows reloading onto a different rank count
This matters for both model weights and sharded optimizer state

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why the naive gather-and-save approach is risky

questions.title: Your first on-call shift for a training platform
questions.prompt: Tell me about how you'd approach your first on-call shift supporting a team's model training infrastructure, where you're still new to the specific alerts and runbooks. What would you do to prepare, and how would you handle an alert you don't fully understand yet?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes concrete preparation before the shift starts: reading through existing runbooks and recent incident postmortems, confirming escalation paths and who the backup on-call is, and making sure dashboards and alert definitions are bookmarked and at least roughly understood even if not memorized. For an alert that isn't fully understood during the shift itself, the right instinct is to follow the runbook's documented first steps if one exists, triage the blast radius -- is a training job merely stalled versus completely down, is data at risk -- and escalate to the backup or a more senior teammate early rather than guessing at a fix under time pressure, especially since a wrong mitigation on GPU training infrastructure (like killing the wrong job) can waste real, expensive compute time. It also means documenting what was observed and tried, even if the issue is eventually handed off, so the postmortem and the runbook both improve afterward.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before the shift even starts, I'd go through the existing runbooks and recent incident writeups, confirm who my backup is and how to reach them, and make sure I at least roughly understand the dashboards and alert thresholds even if I haven't memorized every one. If an alert fires that I don't fully understand, I'm not going to guess at a fix under pressure -- I'll follow whatever first steps the runbook gives, think about blast radius first (is this just a stalled job or something actually at risk of data loss), and escalate early rather than late, especially on infrastructure where the wrong move, like killing the wrong training job, wastes real compute time I can't get back. Whatever happens, I'd make sure to write down what I saw and tried, so it's useful for a postmortem or for updating the runbook even if I ultimately handed it off.
commonMistakes: Trying to resolve everything solo rather than escalating when genuinely unsure, especially under time pressure
Not reading runbooks or recent incident history before the first shift even starts
Panicking into drastic action, like killing jobs or restarting services, without first understanding blast radius
Failing to document what happened for the next person or for a postmortem
keyPoints: Concrete preparation before the shift: runbooks, escalation paths, dashboards
Triage blast radius before taking any action
Escalate early rather than guessing under pressure
Document the incident for future improvement, even when handed off

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows sound judgment about escalation vs self-resolution

questions.title: Stuck on a GPU driver mismatch for half a day
questions.prompt: You've spent half a day trying to resolve a CUDA/driver version mismatch that's blocking a training job, with no progress. Walk me through how you'd decide when to keep troubleshooting versus asking a teammate for help, and how you'd frame that ask.
questions.modelAnswer: A good answer sets a reasonable time-box going in, rather than an open-ended 'I'll ask when I feel stuck,' and treats half a day without progress on a well-scoped infrastructure problem as a clear signal to ask for help rather than push through alone, especially since a driver/CUDA mismatch is often something a teammate has hit before and can resolve in minutes with the right context. Framing the ask well means being specific: what you were trying to do, the exact error message and driver/CUDA/toolkit versions involved, and what you've already tried and ruled out, so the teammate doesn't have to re-derive the same ground you already covered. It also means treating the exchange as a two-way thing -- documenting the eventual fix somewhere shared, like a wiki or runbook, so the next person who hits the same mismatch doesn't lose another half day.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set a rough time-box for myself going in, rather than letting it be open-ended, and half a day with zero progress on something as specific as a driver/CUDA mismatch is well past the point where I should be asking for help -- someone on the team has very likely hit this exact thing before. When I ask, I try to make it easy for them: here's exactly what I was doing, here's the error and the specific versions involved, here's what I already tried and ruled out, so they're not starting from zero. And once we find the fix, I'd write it down somewhere the team can find it, so the next person doesn't burn another half day on the same thing.
commonMistakes: Treating asking for help as a sign of failure and continuing to grind well past the point of diminishing returns
Asking vaguely without sharing what's already been tried, forcing the teammate to start from zero
Not setting any time-box at all and letting the problem silently consume the whole day
Not documenting the resolution afterward so the same problem recurs for someone else
keyPoints: Set a reasonable time-box for troubleshooting before escalating
Recognize version-mismatch issues as the kind of problem a teammate may have already solved
Frame the ask with specifics: error, versions, what's already been tried
Document the resolution for the team afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows sound judgment about when to ask for help
Gives a concrete, specific framing of the ask
Shows follow-through by documenting for the team

questions.title: Explaining why inference got slower to a non-technical stakeholder
questions.prompt: A product manager asks why the chatbot feature 'feels slower' since last week's change, and you know the real cause is that KV cache memory got tighter under higher concurrent traffic, increasing queuing delay. How would you explain this to them without relying on jargon they won't follow?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer translates the mechanism into a concrete, relatable analogy rather than reciting technical terms -- something like: more people are using the chatbot at once than our servers were originally sized for, so new requests wait in a short line before they even start being answered, the same way a restaurant with more diners than tables seats people slower even though the kitchen itself didn't get any slower. It's honest about the actual cause (more usage, not a code regression) and is specific about what's being done about it, such as adding more serving capacity or tuning how many requests can run at once, and roughly when they can expect it resolved, rather than either over-promising a timeline or hiding behind technical language that leaves the PM unable to communicate the status upward themselves.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip the technical terms entirely and go with an analogy: more people are using the chatbot at once than we originally sized the servers for, so new requests are waiting in a short line before they're even answered -- like a restaurant that got more diners than tables, where the kitchen itself didn't get slower, there's just a longer wait before anyone gets seated. I'd be straightforward that this is a usage-growth problem, not a bug from last week's change, and I'd tell them concretely what we're doing about it, like adding more capacity, and roughly when they should expect it to feel better, so they can relay that to whoever's asking them.
commonMistakes: Leading with the jargon itself (KV cache, memory pressure, queuing) and losing the stakeholder immediately
Being vague about the cause in a way that sounds like deflection rather than a clear, honest explanation
Failing to connect the explanation to a concrete next step or timeline the stakeholder can relay onward
Downplaying a real capacity problem to avoid an uncomfortable conversation
keyPoints: Translate the technical mechanism into a concrete, relatable analogy
Be honest about the actual root cause without hiding behind jargon
Connect the explanation to a specific next step or timeline
The stakeholder should come away able to explain the gist to someone else

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Connects it to a concrete next step
Clarity and relatability of the analogy

questions.title: Getting pushback on a pull request you were confident in
questions.prompt: You submit a pull request changing how a training job's checkpoints are saved, confident in the approach, and a senior teammate leaves several comments pointing out it doesn't handle a failure case you hadn't considered. How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the feedback as the review doing its job, not as a personal critique, and starts by actually understanding the failure case being raised -- asking a clarifying question if the scenario isn't immediately obvious, rather than defending the original approach reflexively before fully grasping the concern. If the reviewer is right, the right move is to say so plainly, fix it, and thank them for catching something that could have caused a real incident, since a bad checkpoint silently corrupting a long training run is exactly the kind of bug worth catching in review rather than in production. If there's a genuine disagreement about tradeoffs rather than a clear bug, the response is a substantive counter-argument with reasoning, not a dismissal, and if it still isn't resolved, escalating to a quick conversation rather than a long comment thread is usually faster and less adversarial.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually understand the failure case they're pointing at, not defend my approach before I've fully grasped it -- if it's not obvious, I'll ask a clarifying question. If they're right, I say so directly, thank them for catching it, and fix it; a bad checkpoint silently corrupting a long training run is exactly the kind of thing I'd rather have caught in review than in production. If it's more of a genuine tradeoff disagreement than a clear bug, I'll make my case with actual reasoning rather than just restating my original opinion, and if we're still stuck after a round or two of comments, I'd rather hop on a quick call than let it drag out in writing.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive and arguing from ego rather than engaging with the specific failure case raised
Assuming seniority alone means the reviewer is automatically right without actually verifying the concern
Silently fixing the code without acknowledging the feedback, which erodes trust over time
Letting a disagreement drag out in comment threads instead of having a quick synchronous conversation
keyPoints: Treat review feedback as the process working, not a personal attack
Verify the concern is real before responding either way
Acknowledge being wrong plainly when it's deserved
Escalate to a conversation rather than a long comment war when stuck

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a sound process for verifying and responding to the concern

questions.title: Triaging a pile of small platform tickets
questions.prompt: Your ML platform team has a backlog of a dozen small tickets -- a flaky alert, a slow dashboard, two feature requests from different data science teams, and a minor security finding from an audit. How would you decide what to work on first?
questions.modelAnswer: A sound approach separates tickets by actual risk and blast radius rather than working through them in arrival order: the security finding and the flaky alert both deserve a first look, since a security issue can have compliance or breach implications regardless of how minor it looks on paper, and a flaky alert erodes trust in the whole alerting system every time it fires wrongly, which leads to alert fatigue where real incidents get ignored too. The two feature requests should be weighed by how many people they unblock and how urgent each requesting team's own deadline actually is, which usually means a short conversation with both teams rather than guessing. The slow dashboard, while annoying, is probably the lowest-risk item unless it's actively causing people to miss real signals. The output of this triage should be communicated back to whoever filed each ticket, even the ones going last, so nothing silently falls off the backlog without the requester knowing why.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just work the backlog in the order it came in -- I'd sort by actual risk first. The security finding gets a real look regardless of how minor it sounds, since 'minor' security issues can still have compliance implications, and the flaky alert matters too because every false alarm chips away at trust in the whole alerting system, which eventually means people start ignoring real incidents. For the two feature requests, I'd actually talk to both requesting teams rather than guess at urgency, and weigh them by how many people each one unblocks. The slow dashboard is probably last unless it's actually causing people to miss something important. And whatever order I land on, I'd tell every requester where their ticket landed and why, so nothing just silently disappears from the backlog on them.
commonMistakes: Working tickets in arrival order or by whichever is easiest to close quickly
Treating a security finding as automatically lowest priority just because it's described as minor
Not talking to the requesting teams to understand real urgency before deciding priority
Silently deprioritizing tickets without communicating back to whoever filed them
keyPoints: Triage by risk/blast-radius first, not arrival order or ease
A flaky alert and a security finding both deserve early attention
Weigh feature requests by actual impact and urgency, confirmed with the requesting teams
Communicate the prioritization decision back to everyone, not just the people whose ticket moved up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows sound prioritization reasoning (risk/impact over convenience)
Recognizes the importance of checking in with requesters
Communicates the decision back to the team

questions.title: Disagreeing with a teammate over how to fix a flaky training job
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to fix a flaky distributed training job by simply increasing the NCCL timeout, while you suspect the real problem is a genuinely failing GPU on one node. How do you raise your disagreement productively?
questions.modelAnswer: A good answer leads with curiosity and evidence rather than simply asserting a different opinion -- asking what led the teammate to the timeout theory, and sharing the specific evidence pointing at a hardware issue instead, like recurring Xid errors in the driver log on one particular node, or that same node always being the straggler when the job hangs. The goal is proposing a quick, low-cost way to settle the disagreement with data rather than debate, such as cordoning the suspect node for one run and seeing if the flakiness disappears, rather than just repeating competing opinions back and forth. If the teammate's fix is also reasonable as an interim mitigation while the real cause is investigated, it's worth saying so explicitly rather than treating it as an either/or, since the two aren't actually mutually exclusive.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by asking what led them to the timeout theory, rather than just countering with my own guess, and then share the specific evidence I have -- if I'm seeing recurring Xid errors on one particular node, or that node is consistently the straggler whenever the job hangs, that's worth putting on the table concretely. From there I'd propose something cheap that settles it with data instead of opinions, like cordoning that one node for a run and seeing if the flakiness goes away. And honestly, raising the timeout isn't necessarily wrong either -- it could be a reasonable interim mitigation while we figure out the real cause, so I'd say that explicitly rather than framing it as 'my theory versus yours.'
commonMistakes: Treating a technical disagreement as a status contest to win rather than a question to resolve with evidence
Dismissing the teammate's theory without first understanding their reasoning
Not proposing a cheap, concrete way to test either theory, leaving the disagreement stuck at the opinion level
Framing the two approaches as mutually exclusive when one could be a reasonable interim step alongside investigating the other
keyPoints: Lead with curiosity about the teammate's reasoning, not a competing assertion
Bring concrete evidence, like logs or patterns, rather than just a different opinion
Propose a cheap way to test and resolve the disagreement with data
Recognize when two approaches are complementary rather than mutually exclusive

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Approaches the disagreement with curiosity and evidence rather than ego
Proposes a concrete way to resolve it

questions.title: Owning a mistake that caused a wasted training run
questions.prompt: You pushed a config change that, combined with an edge case you hadn't considered, caused a multi-hour distributed training run to silently train on a corrupted data shard before anyone noticed. How would you handle telling your team about this, and what would you do afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: The right first move is proactively surfacing the mistake as soon as it's discovered, rather than waiting to be found out or hoping it goes unnoticed -- a clear, factual account of what happened, when, and the actual impact, such as the hours of compute wasted and whether any model was promoted based on the bad run, without minimizing it or getting defensive about the mistake itself. Afterward, the constructive move is writing or contributing to a blameless postmortem that focuses on the timeline and systemic gaps, like why the corrupted shard wasn't caught by an existing data-validation check if there even is one, and proposing a concrete follow-up, such as adding an automated data-integrity check before training starts, so the same class of mistake can't silently recur. The point isn't self-flagellation; it's turning one incident into a system-level improvement that protects the next person who might make a similar edge-case mistake.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd surface it myself as soon as I realized what happened, rather than hoping nobody notices -- a clear, factual rundown of what happened, when, and what it actually cost us, including whether anything downstream got affected by the bad run. After that, I'd want to write up a blameless postmortem focused on the timeline and the systemic gap, not on how badly I feel about it -- the real question is why didn't an existing check catch a corrupted shard before it burned several hours of compute, and if there isn't one, that's the concrete thing to fix. I'd rather turn my mistake into an automated check that protects the next person than just apologize and move on.
commonMistakes: Delaying disclosure in the hope the mistake goes unnoticed, which erodes trust far more than the original mistake would have
Being defensive or minimizing the impact when describing what happened
Treating the postmortem as a forum for self-blame rather than identifying the systemic gap that let it happen
Not following through on a concrete preventive action afterward
keyPoints: Proactively disclose the mistake promptly and factually, without minimizing it
Participate in a blameless postmortem focused on systemic causes, not blame
Propose a concrete preventive fix, such as an automated validation check
Follow through so the mistake doesn't silently recur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a constructive, blameless postmortem framing

questions.title: Staying effective during a live production inference outage
questions.prompt: It's your first time on-call during a real incident: the inference serving endpoint is returning errors for a meaningful share of users, and people in the incident channel are asking for updates every few minutes. How do you stay effective instead of getting overwhelmed?
questions.modelAnswer: Staying effective here means separating two different jobs that are easy to conflate under pressure -- actually diagnosing and fixing the issue, and communicating status to the people asking -- and not letting the second one derail the first. A practical way to do this is giving a quick, honest status update up front, such as 'investigating, will update again in 10 minutes,' that buys uninterrupted focus time, rather than trying to answer every individual question in real time while also debugging. It also means working through triage systematically rather than randomly trying fixes under pressure -- checking the most likely and cheapest things first, like recent deploys, dependency health, and resource exhaustion, before reaching for riskier interventions -- and asking for a second pair of hands early if the cause isn't obvious within a few minutes, rather than trying to be the hero who solves it alone while the error rate climbs.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd do is separate debugging from communicating, because trying to do both in real time is how I'd get overwhelmed. I'd post something like 'investigating now, next update in 10 minutes' right away, which buys me uninterrupted time instead of answering every message as it comes in. Then I'd triage systematically -- recent deploys, dependency health, obvious resource exhaustion -- starting with the cheap, likely causes before reaching for anything risky. And if I'm not making progress within a few minutes, I'd ask for a second pair of hands rather than trying to be the one person who solves it alone while the error rate keeps climbing.
commonMistakes: Trying to answer every incident-channel message in real time while also debugging, fragmenting attention on both
Jumping straight to a risky fix under pressure without first checking cheap, likely causes
Treating asking for help during an incident as a sign of weakness rather than the fastest path to resolution
Going quiet for long stretches without any status update, increasing anxiety and duplicate 'any update?' messages
keyPoints: Separate diagnosing/fixing from stakeholder communication, protecting focus time with a proactive status update
Triage systematically from cheap/likely causes to riskier ones
Ask for help early rather than trying to solve it alone under pressure
Keep a steady cadence of brief updates rather than going silent or over-communicating

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows a sound approach to balancing communication and diagnosis
Recognizes the value of asking for help early
